chunks: "I'd say the question mixes up two things. An inductor doesn't limit how big the current gets, it limits how fast it can change.
The law is v equals L di over dt , so the current can't jump, it ramps at V over L . That's still a ramp, and for a motor winding L is tiny.
A small 12 volts motor with 1 millihenries has an initial slope of 12 volts over a millihenry, which is 12 amps per millisecond. The final value isn't set by the inductor at all.
At standstill there's no back-EMF, so the only thing limiting current is the winding resistance, V over R .
With 2 ohms that's 6 amps, versus a few hundred milliamps once it's spinning. The time to get there is L over R , here half a millisecond. So it's not a contradiction.
The current is continuous, it starts at zero, but on the scale of the electronics it rises extremely fast, to a value that's many times the running current.
And the rotor is far slower than that: its mechanical time constant is milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, so the back-EMF that would rein the current in hasn't built up yet.
That's the inrush. The inductor just rounds the very front edge of it."
